title: Gandhari
hook: a folded cloth, tied once over a young bride's eyes, and the many ways people have read it since

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhari's answer to her son before battle: where dharma is, there is victory. Did you give someone an honest blessing instead of an easy one? Day one thousand three hundred forty.

Paintings show it. So do films and television. A strip of cloth, tied over Gandhari's eyes. Last year on this path, the story of how it got there was told in passing: a princess of Gandhara learns that the prince she will marry, Dhritarashtra, is blind, and she binds her own eyes. The Mahabharata tells it in a few lines and moves on. Readers have kept coming back to it. Today, Gandhari's blindfold, and the different things people see in it.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `A FEW LINES IN THE EPIC.` → `WHAT PEOPLE SEE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here is what the first book of the Mahabharata gives us, in paraphrase. Gandhari hears that her husband-to-be is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it over, and binds her eyes, resolving not to go beyond her husband. That's it. No speech. No explanation beyond that one resolve. Readers have filled the silence in different ways. Devotional retellings hear devotion: a wife who would not see what her husband could not, and the strength the stories give her for it. Others hear solidarity, sharing his darkness rather than looking down on it. And some modern readers hear something more troubled: a woman of clear sight who chose not to look, at a court that badly needed someone to look. Those readings sit side by side; the epic doesn't settle them. There's also a story people tell, from later retellings. Before his last fight, Gandhari asks Duryodhana to come to her unclothed, so that one look from her long-covered eyes can make his body hard as diamond. He comes, but out of shame covers his waist, and that is where he is struck. It's a story about the power people sensed behind the cloth. What can a reader take from it? First, a choice made once can shape a whole life. Second, a sacrifice can be read many ways at once, and the person making it doesn't control the reading. Third, the cloth isn't the end of Gandhari's sight. In the war's aftermath she will see in other ways, and that is tomorrow's story.
screen: `SHE FOLDS A CLOTH OVER HER EYES` · `DEVOTION, SOLIDARITY, OR NOT LOOKING` · `A STORY OF A DIAMOND BODY` · `ONE CHOICE, MANY READINGS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a moment without sight. Sit comfortably and, if you're somewhere safe, close your eyes, or rest a hand gently over them. Notice how the room changes: the sounds come closer, the body gets louder. Stay here a few breaths. Then ask one quiet question: is there something in my life I've chosen not to look at? Don't open it now. Just notice whether something answers. When you're ready, let your eyes open slowly. If you pray, you can ask to see clearly. The bell holds the time.
Gandhari. Hearing her husband was blind, she bound her own eyes, and readers since have seen devotion, solidarity and refusal in that one cloth. Today's word.
Your line: Gandhari. Today, look straight at one thing you've been choosing not to see, even for a minute, the way readers keep looking at Gandhari's cloth. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: Hindus meet Gandhari's blindfold in retellings of the Mahabharata, on stage and screen and in story, where it is held up as an image of a wife's devotion and, in some modern retellings, questioned.

notes: Confirm the Adi Parva lines: Gandhari folds a cloth many times and binds her eyes, resolving not to exceed (atyasuya) her husband. Section numbers differ between editions.
